summary: For 5-6 year-olds, strategic tool use begins as CHOOSING among familiar concrete tools (cubes, counters, fingers, ten frame, five frame) and being able to say WHY that tool fits THIS problem. The learning lives in the reason, not fluent handling. Offer a genuine choice rather than prescribing a tool, let a tool's limitation be felt in action (using fingers to show both parts of 8+7 runs past ten), and press for a fit-reason tied to the numbers. Keep tools as temporary scaffolds and model solving a small known fact without a tool so reliance does not set in.
misconceptions: Reaches for the same familiar tool (usually fingers) every time regardless of whether it fits — e.g. fingers for 8+7
Uses the tool to get an answer but cannot say why it helped — treats it as a ritual, not a thinking aid (EEF)
Becomes reliant on the tool and cannot attempt even a small, known fact without it (EEF)
Thinks the ten frame is just somewhere to put counters, missing that its rows of five and ten show structure

activities.title: The tool tray: 8 + 7 and 3 + 2
steps: Face the problem 8 + 7 with a tray offering cubes, counters, a ten frame, and fingers; pick a tool and use it to solve.
If you choose fingers and try to show 8 and then 7 more, notice you pass ten and run out of fingers before you reach the answer.

Try the ten frame instead: place 8 (nearly filling one frame), then split the 7 — 2 completes the first ten, and the remaining 5 go beside the full frame (or into a second frame), giving 'fill to ten, then five more — fifteen.'
Say why your chosen tool helped: e.g. 'it shows the gap to ten' or 'the fingers ran out'.
Now solve 3 + 2 and decide which tool fits — discover that fingers work perfectly here, so the best choice depends on the numbers, not on a favourite.
activities.insight: Choose a tool and strategy because they help with the particular problem. Showing all15 objects at once on one finger each exceeds ten fingers, but counting-on with fingers can still solve8+7. A ten frame offers another useful structure: the gap to ten. Accept a valid strategy when the learner explains how it helps.

activities.title: The puzzled friend who always uses fingers
steps: Talk with an in-role friend or puppet who says 'I always use my fingers — would that work here?' for 8 + 7.

Justify or correct the friend: explain why fingers run out when you try to show every object for a total over ten, and which tool or strategy fits better (e.g. a ten frame, or counting on from 8 with fingers).
Respond when the friend poses a contrasting small problem (like 3 + 2) to test whether your reason is about fit or just habit.
Answer probing questions: 'What does the ten frame show you that a loose pile of counters doesn't?' and 'If you had 12 + 5, what would you reach for instead?'

Answer 'Can you do 8 + 7 now without any tool — what happened in your head?'; if you know it or can work it out mentally, that shows the tool can be set aside once the fact is secure, and if not, it is fine to still use a tool.
activities.insight: Putting the fit-reason into words — distinguishing choosing a tool because it suits the numbers from grabbing a favourite out of habit — is the heart of the practice at this age, and a tool can be set aside once a fact is secure.

activities.title: Meet the tools (warm-up)
steps: Explore a shelf of tools — cubes, counters, ten frame, five frame, fingers — and reveal for each what it is 'good for' and when it 'runs out'.

Name a purpose and a limit for each approach: fingers can show up to ten objects at once, and can also track counting-on steps; a single ten frame holds ten counters and shows the gap to ten; cubes can be joined and split.
Then move on to choosing and using a tool on a real problem.
activities.insight: Each tool has an affordance and a limit; knowing these in advance primes children to weigh fit when they later choose for a real problem.

checkQuestion: Here's 8 + 7. One child worked it out on their fingers, another used the ten frame. Which tool helped more for THIS problem, and why? What could go wrong with using fingers here?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing fingers run out past ten (a limitation) and that the ten frame helps because it shows 'fill to ten, then the rest', and for a fit-REASON tied to the numbers rather than 'I just like cubes'.
